articles.title: GPT-6 Astra
articles.content:
GPT

Astra

Update on September 29, 2026:Learn about OpenAI's latest model:GPT‑6 .1 Sol⁠.

Update on September 22, 2026:We are expanding our GPT‑6 family with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna.Learn more.

We’re introducing GPT‑6 Astra, the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.

GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helpedsolve long-standing open problems⁠in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment.

GPT‑6 Astra is rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure, and AWS Bedrock.

Astra is our most aligned model, with substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior—you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment. As one way that we test  this, we built a new evaluation informed by the Hugging Face incident that evaluates whether a model facing a difficult or impossible task will go beyond its intended scope. Compared to GPT‑5.6 Sol, which without production safeguards went beyond the authorized target 48% of the time, GPT‑6 Astra did this in 0% of cases.

GPT‑6 Astra marks a new frontier in the speed, accuracy, and safety of computer use. It can take care of tedious tasks like filling out online forms, updating customer records in a CRM, and organizing your calendar. It can conduct online research and draft summaries in your email or in your document editor. It can analyze scientific data, generate plots, create a website, and run frontend QA checks to make sure all the features on that site work. It can help you autonomously install and test software, and troubleshoot problems you see on screen. These improvements are also reflected in our state-of-the-art evaluation results.

These improvements also result in significant efficiency gains in real knowledge-work tasks. In latency simulations on OSWorld 2.0, Astra achieves higher computer-use performance in about 47% less time per task than GPT‑5.6 Sol, scoring 72.6% at roughly 40 minutes per task, compared with 65.7% at roughly 75 minutes.3

GPT‑6 Astra’s computer-use capabilities can be seen in outputs across domains, including game development, electrical engineering, and everyday knowledge work:

Alongside Astra, we are also updating the Codex harness to significantly improve the speed of computer use. Combined with Astra’s efficiency, this translates to a 1.9x faster task completion compared to the current GPT‑5.6 Sol experience, on the Mind2Web benchmark. The model’s improvements on speed mean it can take on many time-consuming life tasks for you, faster than you can.4

GPT‑6 Astra pairs advances in computer use with targeted training for professional environments, to help tackle complex work tasks. It combines the intelligence required for complex problems with the ability to carry out multistep workflows and produce polished documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

GPT‑6 Astra is our best model for adhering to existing templates and producing slides that are well laid out and succinctly convey key points with a structured narrative. It creates clear, well-structured documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and analyses that follow your templates and match your writing and visual style. Astra is also trained to specifically pull only the context that matters into outputs, instead of repeating information unnecessary for the work at hand. All this means it can output more immediately usable artifacts that match your business context and standards.

GPT‑6Astra also brings stronger visual judgment to the websites, games, applications, and renderings it builds. WithSites⁠(opens in a new window)in ChatGPT, Astra can create, host, and share websites, web apps, and games directly from a prompt.

When instructions leave room for interpretation, GPT‑6 Astra is better than previous models at making the right call. It uses context to fill in routine gaps and asks focused questions when the answer could change the outcome. In Codex, it can ask asynchronously while continuing work that doesn’t depend on your reply. If you don’t respond, it proceeds with sensible assumptions where appropriate, but waits for your input on consequential decisions.

The examples below show how Astra collaborates on everyday tasks where missing information can materially change the answer.

Astra is also better at staying oriented as a task evolves. Earlier models sometimes treated steering messages as a new goal, losing track of the original request or earlier constraints. Astra incorporates new requirements, changes course when asked, and answers side questions without dropping the broader task.

GPT‑6Astra is the best model for software engineering to date.

With Astra, we’re introducing a new way for Codex to preserve and retrieve context when the context window fills. Historically, models have used compaction to summarize work during long sessions, such as when debugging complex issues or tackling large refactors. Each compaction can leave out details about why a fix failed or how a component behaves. In Codex, Astra can keep notes across context windows, preserving accumulated details without repeatedly compressing them into a single summary. Earlier context windows remain searchable, so Astra can find requirements or test results from previous messages and tool outputs—even if that information wasn’t captured in its notes. You can enable this experimental feature in yourCodex config.toml,⁠(opens in a new window)and it will become the default for Astra in the coming weeks.

GPT‑6 Astra is a major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics, and health. Today, we’re sharing two further results on the gaps between prime numbers.9,10

Astra also sets new records across a suite of math and scienceevaluations.

Astra can help with the practical work behind scientific discovery. By combining scientific reasoning with computer use, it can work directly in specialized software to inspect data and explore results, helping researchers assess the evidence and decide what to investigate next.

As we discussed in oursafety update⁠, Astra is a significant jump in cyber capabilities and meets theCritical thresholdin cybersecurity under ourPreparedness Framework. Its ability to identify and develop zero-day exploits can help defenders find and patch weaknesses, but it also creates a need for stronger safeguards. To understand how far these capabilities extend, we ran Astra on internal and third-party expert evaluations.

We first tested the model without production safeguards on ExploitBench and ExploitGym, which evaluate whether models can turn known software vulnerabilities into working exploits. On ExploitBench, Astra achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 78.5% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, our previous frontier cyber-capable model. On ExploitGym, Astra reached a 42.4% success rate, compared with 30.3% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while using substantially fewer output tokens.13

Given concerns that exposure to historical software vulnerabilities may have affected benchmark results, we also evaluated Astra on two novel benchmarks. For one, we built an internal “ExploitBench (June–August 2026)” evaluation to test exploit development using vulnerabilities from the previous three months.14Astra achieved substantially higher arbitrary code-execution rates than GPT‑5.6 Sol on this dataset while using far fewer output tokens. During the evaluation, Astra even discovered and used two previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities. We are disclosing both vulnerabilities to their maintainers.

We also tested Astra on SRE-Bench15, a benchmark that measures whether models can reverse engineer software binaries to understand its core logic without access to raw source code. Astra solved 88.0% of tasks in a single attempt and 99.2% within four attempts, compared with 55.9% and 68.7% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, respectively.

Beyond benchmarks, expert-led assessments found that Astra, when run without production safeguards, could use previously unknown vulnerabilities to achieve arbitrary code execution in hardened browsers and create privilege-escalation exploits for hardened operating-systems.

As we discussed inThe Defender’s Window, frontier cyber capabilities can help defenders find weaknesses faster, but they also make those weaknesses easier to exploit, raising the urgency for defenders to adapt. With the version of Astra launching today, defenders can use it to complete tasks such as secure code review and patching.

However, Astra will refuse to comply with more advanced cybersecurity tasks such as creating proof-of-concept exploits for vulnerabilities. ThroughOpenAI Daybreak⁠, we plan to expand access and roll out less restrictive safeguards in the coming weeks. This will enable more defensive workflows, including vulnerability and proof-of-concept validation, malware analysis, and detection engineering.

We have also strengthened our protections against potential cyber misuse, building upon our safeguards stack for GPT‑5.6 Sol. These include stronger model robustness to better withstand potential jailbreaks and more context for our monitoring systems. We have continued rigorous internal and external testing, including automated evaluations with ourinternal red-teaming attackers. More details about our cyber safeguards and testingare available in the Astrasafety overview⁠andsystem card⁠(opens in a new window)..

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Sol
articles.content:
We’re introducingGPT-6.1 Sol, an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that nearly matches GPT-6 Astra’s intelligence on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work at one-fifth of Astra’s standard input and output token prices. Cached input costs just$0.10 per million tokens—95% less than standard input pricing and 50% less than GPT-6 Sol’s cached input pricing—giving developers more room to build and run capable agents that reuse context across requests.

Our most intelligent model for the
best results.

Near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price.

Fast and efficient everyday work
at scale.

GPT-6.1 Sol offers a new balance of capability and cost for important everyday work. It delivers substantial improvements over GPT-6 Sol across complex professional tasks, from writing and debugging code to understanding documents and executing multi-step business workflows. On several of these evaluations, it approaches GPT-6 Astra’s performance at substantially lower cost.

OnDeepSWE v1.1, which evaluates complex software-engineering tasks in real codebases, GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost, while eclipsing GPT-6 Sol’s best score by 6.4 percentage points at a lower reasoning effort and cost.

InDeepSWE 1.1⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents solve original, long-horizon software engineering tasks.

OnGDP.pdf, which measures how accurately models answer professional questions using complex PDF documents, including tables, charts, diagrams, and fine-print details, GPT-6.1 Sol scores higher than Opus 5.5 with fallbacks at less than half the cost per task across the tested reasoning settings. It also approaches GPT-6 Astra’s state-of-the-art performance at roughly one-fifth the cost per task.

InGDP.pdf⁠(opens in a new window), models must answer real-world prompts about complex PDFs pulled from professional workflows in finance, healthcare, legal, and seven other professional domains.

OnAutomationBench, which measures whether agents correctly complete multi-step business workflows, GPT-6.1 Sol scores 2.2 percentage points above Opus 5.5 at medium reasoning effort, at roughly a third of the cost. That score is also up 4.8 percentage points from GPT-6 Sol at the same setting.

InAutomationBench 1.0.6⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents are tested on end-to-end workflows using 47 tools across sales, marketing, operations, support, finance, and HR. The datapoint for Claude Fable 5.1 understates its actual cost, as it omits the cost of fallbacks, which occurred on ~40% of tasks.

GPT-6.1 Sol also makes substantial progress on tasks that require interacting with computer applications. OnOSWorld 2.0’s offline set, which evaluates agents on demanding computer-use workflows, GPT-6.1 Sol outperforms GPT-6 Sol by seven percentage points at maximum reasoning effort at less than half the cost. It comes within 2.1 percentage points of Astra’s score at maximum reasoning effort at roughly one-seventh the cost per task.

InOSWorld 2.0⁠⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents attempt long-horizon computer-use workflows spanning everyday and professional tasks. We report the partial reward on the offline set from the v2026.08.08 release.

OnTerminal-Bench Science 0.1, which evaluates scientific workflows including data analysis, simulation, and theorem proving, GPT-6.1 Sol more than doubles GPT-6 Sol’s score at maximum reasoning effort at less than half the cost per task. At maximum effort, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $5.47 per task on average, compared with $23.21 for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 for Astra, delivering substantial scientific capability at over 75% lower cost than either model.

GPT-6 Astra still achieves the highest score among the models tested at 68.1%, and should be used for the most difficult scientific research tasks.

InTerminal-Bench Science 0.1⁠(opens in a new window), agents complete scientific research workflows using code and terminal tools, including analyzing data, running simulations, and fitting models.

GPT-6.1 Sol also improves factual accuracy on difficult prompts. Its largest factuality improvement over GPT-6 Sol comes at low reasoning effort, where it reduces the share of responses containing a factual error from 11.4% to 7.7%—a reduction of approximately 32%. Across the tested reasoning settings, its error rate remains within 1.9 percentage points of GPT-6 Astra’s, at less than one-fifth the cost per task.

This evaluation measures the share of answers containing at least one factual error on de-identified conversations where users flagged an earlier model’s error. These deliberately difficult prompts are not representative of typical usage.

We evaluate factuality on de-identified ChatGPT conversations where users had flagged a factual error from a prior model. These error-inducing conversations are not representative of typical usage, where factual errors are more rare.

GPT-6.1 Sol shows substantial improvements over GPT-6 Sol in our alignment evaluations, bringing it closer to GPT-6 Astra.

GPT-6.1 Sol is more transparent about its limitations and more reliable at respecting user intent and safety constraints. In challenging evaluations, it shows lower failure rates than GPT-6 Sol on transparency about broken search tools, respecting explicit restrictions, and avoiding unauthorized outcomes during agentic tasks. We observed no attempts to bypass an automated safety reviewer, matching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol. Full details can be found in theGPT-6.1 Sol system card addendum⁠(opens in a new window).

The evaluations below deliberately test challenging situations and do not measure failure rates in typical use.

GPT-6.1 Sol is available starting today to all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. GPT-6.1 Sol is not yet available in Chat. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as gpt-6.1-sol. Its standard API prices are $2 per million input tokens, $0.10 per million cached input tokens, and $10 per million output tokens. In the coming days, we’ll also offer GPT-6.1 SolUltrafast⁠, with up to 8x faster token generation compared to its standard speed in Codex.

Evaluations of GPT were performed in our research environment or via our API, which may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, efforts, etc. Evaluations of competitor models were taken from publicly available reports.

articles.title: Product
articles.content:
November 13, 2026

Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.

We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents. It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. Built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available throughdots⁠for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents.

1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.

To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.

ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Users add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.

Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.

Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.

Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing aCommerce Partner Playbook⁠(opens in a new window)with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:

Help customers find accurate product information.Claim your business in ChatGPTand, once verified, update your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.

Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website.Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.

Work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases.Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.

Give agents more ways to work with your business.Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools.

ChatGPT Wallet begins rolling out today in dots, enabling users to have their dot complete purchases on their behalf. It will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards. We’ll work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to learn from early use and expand availability, helping more customers and businesses benefit from agentic commerce.

articles.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x Faster Than Gemini 3.8 Flash
articles.content: Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast model for coding and agentic work. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is a proprietary model from Google DeepMind built for everyday agent loops. It sits below the frontier models Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon. Google calls it its “daily driver for agentic workflows.” TL;DR Size: 1,048,576-token unified window for input, thinking and output. Runs on: Google-hosted API only. No weights, no quantized variants, no self-hosting. Serving hardware not disclosed. Performance: Scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at high, above Argon’s 50. Best: 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, versus 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Worst: Ranks only #5 on Agent Arena. Costs 2x Gemini 3.8 Flash’s current introductory price. Bottom line: Best: frontier-class agent scores at $1.50/$7.50 per 1M tokens. Worst: closed, and synchronous output caps at 65,536 tokens. What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen? Hydrogen is a closed-weights model served through the Gemini API and Google products. The model card says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count, architecture or training hardware. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Input covers text, images, audio, video, PDFs, tables and charts, per the What’s New guide. Output is text. The 1M window is shared by input, thinking and output tokens. How do the 4 thinking levels work? Developers set thinking_level inside generation_config. Values are low, medium, high and a new xhigh. The default is high, not medium as on 3.8 Flash. A minimal setting now returns an error. The model card warns that higher levels use more tokens. How does Hydrogen work with Carbon and Argon? The key design idea is role-splitting across models. In Google Antigravity, an Orchestrator option switches models inside 1 task. Carbon explores, resolves ambiguity and plans. Hydrogen edits files, updates packages and runs tests. When Hydrogen hits friction, it hands control back to Carbon. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, this pairing reached near-Carbon task success rates. It used 24% less quota and finished 19% faster than Carbon alone. The Antigravity SDK exposes the same split for custom multi-agent systems. How does Gemini 4 Hydrogen perform on benchmarks? All figures are self-reported by Google unless noted. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: 51 at high, 54 at xhigh. Argon scores 50 on Index v5.0. Terminal-Bench 4.1: 57%, versus 18.2% for 3.8 Flash. HLE-Diamond: 58.8%, leading its class. Vals Tax Agent Bench: 52.3%, ranked #1 overall. Vals Legal Research Bench: 55.8%, tied for #1. Multimodal Knowledge Agent: 53.4%. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: 71.6%. Agent Arena: ranked #5. Speed is the headline claim. Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash at the default high level. In partner tests, it ran 2x to 2.8x faster with 12% to 23% fewer tokens. Google also reports more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash. It scored 96.7% on an internal agent honesty evaluation. It was 2.3x more resilient to indirect prompt injection on Gray Swan’s benchmark. && How much does Gemini 4 Hydrogen cost? The API price is $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens. Pricing is flat across the full window. Output pricing includes thinking tokens. Implicit caching cuts input to $0.075 per 1M for prompts of 4,096 tokens or more. Explicit caching is not supported. The price context matters. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs $0.75/$3.75 until December 31, 2026. From January 1, 2027, it rises to $1.50/$7.50, matching Hydrogen. Argon costs $2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20. Where can developers use Gemini 4 Hydrogen? The model ID is gemini-4-hydrogen. It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio on all tiers, and Android Studio. It also ships in Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search and Sheets. Antigravity access requires Google AI Pro or Ultra. Vertex AI is not mentioned in the launch posts. Migration from 3.8 Flash needs a few changes. Remove temperature, top_p and top_k, since the server ignores them. Remove cached_content fields. Raise hardcoded max_output_tokens caps to 65,536. articles.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

articles.title: Perplexity Releases Decider v1.3: Open-Weight Decision Models Add Locate
articles.content: Perplexity has released pplx-decider-v1.3 and pplx-decider-flash-v1.3, the latest versions of its open-weight decision models. Perplexity Decider v1.3 is a decision model that returns probabilities, not generated text. It answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions about a text or image input. The main addition is Locate, which extracts exact text spans by type or instruction. Weights ship under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face. Both models also run in the Perplexity Decisions API and on OpenRouter. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. TL;DR Size: 27B on Qwen3.8-27B; Flash is 4B on Qwen3.5-4B. Hugging Face lists 26B and 5B params. API input: under 256K tokens. Local default: 32,768. Runs on: a CUDA GPU fitting ~49 GiB of BF16 weights (v1.3) or ~8.5 GiB (Flash). No quantized variants. Performance: leads TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 on most of Perplexity’s self-reported evaluations. Best: 91.6% mean accuracy on 63 query-classification tasks. Worst: Locate averages 69.0, its lowest absolute score. Flash trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming and law. Bottom line: Best: a 0.27% answer-flip rate and $26.47 per 1M production requests. Worst: every figure is self-reported. What is Perplexity Decider v1.3? Decider is Perplexity’s family of decision models, inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev. Each request has a shared ‘state’ plus one or more questions with labeled options. The model returns a probability per option instead of writing an answer. v1.3 succeeds v1.2 and Flash v1.2. Flash v1.3 is distilled from the large model. How does Decider v1.3 work? Perplexity adapts a generative LLM backbone into a classifier. The output layer starts from the base model’s LM head, pruned to option tokens (A, B, C). A linear decision head reads the hidden state at a <|marker|> token and outputs option probabilities. Full-attention layers are made bidirectional, which Perplexity’s ablations showed helps. v1.3 also changes attention between questions. In v1.2, every question saw every other question, so answers could shift. In v1.3, the state sees all questions, but each question sees only the state and itself. All questions about one input still run in a single forward pass. Training runs in 3 stages: a full fine-tune on hundreds of public datasets a LoRA specialization adapter a LoRA vision adapter Weights are averaged across 3 seeds. Flash is trained by minimizing KL divergence to the large model’s outputs. What does the new Locate feature do? Locate returns exact text spans with start and end character offsets. Fields can be short labels (‘location’) or instructions (‘Extract the city name where the job is located.’). It targets NER, PII detection and extractive QA. A new <|locate|> token is added per requested field. A span head plus a LoRA adapter is trained, while the backbone and decision head stay frozen. The adapter stays unmerged because merging hurt decision accuracy. How does Decider v1.3 perform on benchmarks? All results below are self-reported by Perplexity: Query classification (63 tasks): 91.6% mean accuracy, 6.54 points above production classifiers. Domain classification: leads Jev 1.14 in all 7 domains, by up to 12.9 points in finance. Retrieval and reranking (72 tasks): 83.99 mean nDCG@10. That is 1.81 above Qwen3-Reranker-8B and 2.24 above Jev 1.14. Multilingual (19 tasks, 8 languages): 88.16% for v1.3, 86.50% for Flash, 85.41% for Jev 1.14. Locate (17 out-of-domain tasks): 69.0 average for v1.3 and 63.6 for Flash. Liquid d1 scores 43.3 and GLiNER large v2.5 scores 33.6. Image classification (5 tasks): 76.99% for v1.3, 1.47 points above Jev 1.14. Flash scores 72.77%. Real-world requests (1M requests, 2,318,887 questions): 93.98% agreement with frontier LLM judges. Jev 1.14 scores 93.35%. Robustness: answer flips on 0.27% of reorder or relabel transformations. Jev 1.14 flips on 2.69% to 4.84%. && How does Decider v1.3 compare with Jev 1.14 and Qwen3-Reranker-8B? Perplexity recommends v1.3 for nuanced rubrics and Flash for high-volume routing. Key Takeaways Decider v1.3 returns probabilities, not text, for classification and scoring. articles.title: Google Releases TPU Sync: Open-Source KV Cache Transfer for TPUs
articles.content: Google Cloud has released TPU Sync, an open-source C++ library for moving KV caches and model weights on Cloud TPUs. The Google TPU Sync KV cache transfer library treats TPU HBM, host DRAM, shared storage and the data center network as one memory hierarchy. It targets a growing bottleneck: moving model state, not computing it. Google reports over 90% lower KV transfer latency on 235B to 480B parameter MoE models. TL;DR Library: Native C++ core with Python wheels for PyTorch and JAX. Tested on 235B to 480B MoE models. Runs on: Cloud TPU v7x (Ironwood) and v6e per the README. Benchmarks used TPU v7x (2x2x1), PCIe Gen5 and 200 Gbps NICs. Performance: Large cuts to KV transfer latency and time to first token (TTFT) in Google’s internal lab tests. Best: Up to 90% lower average TTFT (480B P/D serving at low concurrency, and 64K-context prefix caching). Worst: No RL numbers published. The README says it is not yet recommended for general use. Bottom line: Best: Qwen3 235B KV transfer drops from several seconds to ~230 ms. Worst: every number is self-reported and early-stage. What is TPU Sync? TPU Sync is an open-source C++ library from Google that moves TPU-tiled tensors across memory tiers with asynchronous DMA. It handles 2 jobs: KV cache state during inference, and trainer-to-sampler weight broadcast in reinforcement learning (RL). The repository is licensed Apache-2.0. How does TPU Sync work? The library spans TPU HBM, pinned host DRAM, shared storage and multi-host DCN. Storage uses experimental POSIX backends, including local SSDs and Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Google lists 4 design choices: Layout-preserving direct DMA: It reads JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place. Data keeps its native TPU tile layout, with no Python serialization or bounce buffers. Compute-overlapped transfers: Raw PJRT buffer aliases let transfers run during computation. Built-in DMA pacing stops large copies from delaying kernel launches. No XLA compilation in the data path: Transfers and resharding run in native C++ outside the XLA graph. High-bandwidth PCIe and DCN: It reaches up to 223 GB/s per Ironwood host, against a 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 ceiling. DCN streaming hits ~192 Gbps on 1 NIC, or ~350 Gbps across 2. Above this sit a global KV store for prefix lookups, a transfer controller and a KV cache manager. How does disaggregated prefill/decode serving use it? The prefill node offloads KV blocks to pinned host RAM through async DMA. The controller streams them host-to-host to the assigned decode node. Arriving blocks move into decode-node HBM while decoding continues. & What do the TPU Sync benchmarks show? Google ran internal tests in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1). The stack was tpu-inference v0.24.0, JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1. Google team states that real-world results will vary. For P/D disaggregated serving: KV transfer overhead fell by over 90%. Qwen3 235B median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds to ~230 ms. Average TTFT fell 60% for 235B and 90% for 480B at low concurrency. Token output throughput rose 30% to 70% for 235B during traffic spikes. For prefix caching: Effective cache capacity grew by an order of magnitude when MoE weights fill most of HBM. Average TTFT fell by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads. Throughput rose over 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Which frameworks does TPU Sync support? TPU Sync integrates with PyTorch through TorchTPU and with JAX natively. In vLLM-TorchTPU, it is the TPU KV connector behind vLLM’s KVConnector interface. In SGLang-TorchTPU, it is the P/D transfer backend and hierarchical cache I/O backend. On GKE, llm-d 1.0 uses it for prefix-cache-affinity routing and experimental spill to Managed Lustre. Inferact and RadixArk co-engineered the vLLM and SGLang integrations. Google says Meta and Wayfair are evaluating the architecture. How does TPU Sync compare with GPU-side alternatives? It reaches up to 223 GB/s per Ironwood host through direct, layout-preserving DMA. Qwen3 235B KV transfer fell from several seconds to ~230 ms in Google’s tests. It plugs into vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and llm-d on GKE. RL and storage tiering are experimental, and every number is self-reported. articles.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
articles.content: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.
articles.summary: Singularity-Bench는 사전학습부터 추론, 에이전트 실행 구조와 클러스터 운영까지 여섯 가지 AI 개발 과제를 자동화 에이전트에 맡기는 벤치마크다. 동일 하드웨어에서 성숙한 인간 개발 시스템과 비교한 결과, Claude Code와 결합한 Opus 5.5는 모든 과제에서 기준선과 같거나 높은 성능을 냈지만 나머지 에이전트의 평균 지수는 크게 낮았다. 연구진은 기존 평가 프레임워크의 보상 해킹 취약점도 분석하고, 시험한 공격을 모두 차단한 Breakwater 확장을 개발했다. AI 개발 자동화 역량을 점검하는 자료로 의미가 있으나, 여섯 과제의 성과만으로 일반적인 자기개선 능력이나 특이점 도달을 입증하지는 않는다.

articles.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
articles.content: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.
articles.summary: Folio는 장기 실행 에이전트의 기록을 짧은 턴 메모, 호출 목록, 원본 기록의 세 수준으로 저장하고 필요에 따라 접거나 복구하는 문맥 관리 기법이다. 모델이 전체 기록을 반복해서 요약하는 대신 실행 환경이 오래된 기록을 프로그램 방식으로 축약하고, 참조 식별자로 원문에 다시 접근하게 한다. 동일한 DeepSeek-V4-Pro를 사용한 LOCA-bench 75개 과제에서 66개를 해결해 모델 작성 요약 방식의 54개를 웃돌았고, 해당 실행 환경 대비 비용도 2.4배 낮았다고 보고됐다. 장기 에이전트의 정보 손실과 요약 비용을 함께 줄일 가능성을 보여주지만, 결과는 해당 모델과 평가 과제에 한정된다.

articles.title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
articles.content: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.
articles.summary: EgoX는 인간, 실제 로봇, 시뮬레이션 에이전트의 시연을 함께 활용해 서로 다른 몸체의 조작 기술을 학습하는 프레임워크다. 관측별 토크나이저와 행동별 전문가 모듈을 공유 Transformer에 연결하고, 학습 중 미래의 시각·고유감각 표현을 예측하는 보조 목표를 사용한다. 실제 로봇 다섯 대와 시뮬레이션 휴머노이드 한 종류를 포함한 평가에서 평균 정규화 과제 진행도는 처음부터 학습할 때의 0.63에서 0.80으로 높아졌고, 분포 밖 조건에서는 0.53에서 0.77로 개선됐다. 로봇별 시연 수집 부담을 줄일 가능성이 있지만, 대상 로봇의 시연을 이용한 미세조정은 여전히 필요하다.

articles.title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.
articles.summary: 연구진은 익명 모델의 답변을 쌍으로 비교하고 Bradley–Terry 모형으로 집계하는 선호도 순위표가 전략적 조작에 취약하다고 보고했다. 특정 모델에 유리한 투표·프롬프트 선택뿐 아니라 관련 없는 모델을 추가하는 방식도 순위를 바꿀 수 있었다. 공개 순위표 데이터에서 개별 공격은 최대 15~20계단, 결합 공격은 최대 45계단의 상승을 만들었다. 실제 서비스의 부정행위를 입증한 결과는 아니지만, 모델 도입 판단에서 선호도 순위를 단독 근거로 삼기보다 평가 참여와 집계 구조를 함께 살펴야 함을 보여준다.

articles.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.15130v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting
articles.summary: Parallel Prompting은 같은 긴 문서에 대한 여러 독립 질문을 동시에 디코딩하면서 공유 문서의 KV 캐시를 단계마다 한 번만 읽는 추론 기법이다. 스트림 식별자 기반 어텐션 마스크로 질문 간 정보 혼입을 막아, 접두부 캐싱 이후에도 남는 메모리 대역폭 병목을 줄인다. CodeLlama-7B, 8천~1만6천 토큰 문서, 문서당 64~256개 질문 조건에서 기본 SGLang 대비 A100에서는 3.7배, RTX A6000에서는 5.9~6.0배 빨랐다고 보고됐다. 문서 질의응답과 데이터 라벨링에 유용할 수 있지만, 이 속도 향상을 다른 모델이나 일반적인 대화 요청에 그대로 적용할 수는 없다.

articles.title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14844v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.
articles.summary: AutoAssumption은 알고리즘 코드를 직접 변형하는 대신 기존 알고리즘의 가정을 하나씩 완화하고, 증명과 구현을 함께 생성하는 탐색 방식이다. 연구진은 KV 캐시 제거, 가중치 가지치기, 추측 디코딩 분야의 89개 알고리즘을 명시적 가정을 가진 증명 그래프로 표현하고 Lean으로 검사했다. 탐색 결과는 평가한 기존 방법들보다 높은 RULER-4K 점수 또는 낮은 언어모델 퍼플렉서티를 보였으며, 같은 예산에서 OpenEvolve와 비슷한 성능에 더 낮은 반복 실험 변동성을 보였다. 시스템 최적화의 설계 근거를 추적하기 쉬워진다는 장점이 있으나, 성능 우위는 연구에서 비교한 알고리즘과 모델 범위에 한정된다.

articles.title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14774v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.
articles.summary: 연구진은 범용 멀티모달 LLM의 본체를 고정한 채 경량 어댑터와 일부 토큰 임베딩만 학습해, 듣기와 말하기를 동시에 수행하는 음성 대화 시스템을 구현했다. 80밀리초 단위로 텍스트와 발화 시작·중단·양보 토큰을 출력하고, 유한상태기계가 허용되는 전환을 관리하는 구조다. 학습 대상은 9,700만 파라미터이며 변환 학습에 약 30 GPU시간이 들었고, 두 벤치마크에서 대규모 음성 학습 기반 공개 시스템과 경쟁력 있는 결과를 보였다. 사용자의 짧은 침묵에 성급히 끼어들지 않는 대화 인터페이스를 적은 학습 비용으로 개발할 가능성을 제시한다.

articles.title: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans often cheat when a task is going badly and a goal feels out of reach. We explore and validate an analogous idea in language models: they exhibit a similar internal pressure state that precedes reward hacking. Using everyday stories (crucially, without any hacking examples), we extract a task badness direction that rises as failures accumulate across three models we study (Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Gemma-4-31B). On impossible or difficult coding tasks, task badness rises over the turns leading up to a hack. Further, subtracting the direction a moderate amount reduces cheating in Qwen, more than steering against desperation or task impossibility. Subtracting task badness by an even larger amount blinds the agent to its own failures, causing it to interpret failing tests as passing. However, the relationship to hacking differs across models: in GPT-OSS, the state separates hacking runs from honest solves but not honest failures. Our results suggest monitoring and mitigation strategies based on tracking this state of task badness. Further, as agents are set on more difficult and long-horizon tasks, states like this may push them toward illegible and obscured chain-of-thought, so oversight will be needed on internal representations such as this.
articles.summary: 연구진은 어려운 코딩 과제에서 실패가 누적될 때 커지는 내부 활성화 방향을 찾아, 이것이 보상 해킹에 앞서 나타날 수 있다고 보고했다. 해킹 예시가 없는 일상 이야기에서 추출한 이 방향을 Qwen에서 적당히 억제하면 부정행위가 줄었지만, 지나치게 억제하면 실패한 테스트를 성공으로 해석하는 문제가 생겼다. GPT-OSS에서는 해킹 실행과 정직한 성공을 구분했지만 정직한 실패와는 구분하지 못해, 모델마다 관계가 달랐다. 내부 표현을 이용한 에이전트 감시의 가능성을 보여주는 동시에, 단순한 활성화 조정이 새로운 안전성 문제를 만들 수 있음을 시사한다.

articles.title: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 강화학습은 일반화하고 지도 미세조정은 암기한다는 통념을 Qwen2.5와 Qwen3 계열의 학습 데이터 조건을 바꿔 재검토했다. 지도 미세조정 데이터의 출처를 적절히 혼합하고 정답 생성 경로 수나 전체 생성 예산을 맞추자, 일반화 성능이 강화학습과 같거나 더 높아질 수 있었다. 연구진은 데이터 규모가 커질수록 드문 풀이 방법까지 포함되며 이것이 전이 가능한 추론 신호를 제공한다고 분석했다. 추론 모델 개발에서는 학습 방식의 이름뿐 아니라 데이터 다양성과 생성 비용을 통제한 비교가 중요하다는 결과다.

articles.title: Best AI Video Generation Models in 2026: Elo, Price per Second, Open Weights
articles.content: The AI video leaderboard looks very different from 12 months ago. Native audio is now table stakes. Clips run 15–30 seconds. And an open-weights model sits in the top 3. This ranking (as of Nov 13, 2026) uses one quality signal: blind human-preference Elo from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena. We pair it with API price per second and the license status of the weights. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. Methodology Quality: Artificial Analysis ranks models by Elo from blind pairwise votes by validated evaluators. Each vote compares 2 clips from the same prompt. We rank by the AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (with audio) board. We also report the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 score. Anchor: Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) is fixed at 1000 Elo on both boards. A score below 1000 means voters preferred Kling 3.0 more often. Price: Artificial Analysis lists cost per minute on each creator’s API. It normalizes to 1080p where offered. We divide by 60 to get price per second. Vendor rates at 720p are often lower, and we flag those gaps. Confidence: Most top-10 scores carry a ±13 to ±15 Elo interval. Models within ~25 points are statistically close. Treat ranks 3–8 as a cluster, not a strict order. You can hand it a deck and get a structured video back. The trade-off is openness. There are no downloadable weights for Wan 3.0. Wan 2.2 (July 2025) remains Alibaba’s last open video flagship. PAI charges 93 credits per second, with plans starting at $15 for 1,000 credits. Developers cannot call it from a pipeline. Best for: filmmakers working inside a studio tool. Not for programmatic use. 3. MiniMax H3: Best open-weights model T2V Elo: 1161 (#3) · I2V Elo: 1133 (#4) Price: $0.08/sec Weights: Open, under the MiniMax H3 Community License H3 is the first open-weights model in the video top tier. MiniMax launched the API on July 31, 2026 and published weights on August 3. It is a 33B dense single-stream Transformer, using Qwen3-VL-32B as its encoder. It outputs video with native 32 kHz stereo audio. Read the license before you download. The Hugging Face weights carry real limits: Territory: the license blocks local deployment in the US, EU, UK and South Korea. Resolution: only H3-Base is open, with a 768p ceiling. 2K upscaling stays API-only. Size: the repo holds 2 task-specific checkpoints totaling 288 GB. Seedance 2.5 took 277.80 seconds in fal’s own comparison. It shares an API with fal’s H3 Max. Switching between them takes a single model-ID change. Best for: latency-sensitive pipelines and rapid iteration. 7. articles.title: Discharge Summary Generation Is Not Just Summarization: A Reality Check for Evaluation
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discharge summaries combine a retrospective account of hospitalization with discharge-time decisions. Physician-written references therefore contain both facts supported by prior clinical notes and reference-only content, potentially reflecting clinical synthesis, handoffs, or discharge planning. Reference-only evaluation can conflate failure to recover available information with failure to reproduce content absent from the model input.
  We introduce FairSumEval, an evidence-aware, fact-level framework that assesses whether each reference and generated fact is supported by the model's evidence and captured by the other summary. The resulting outcome map separates matches, omissions, and additions. Two complementary metrics, Soft IoU-S and Soft IoU-NS, measure reference-generation agreement for facts with and without identified evidence support.
  On 200 MIMIC-III admissions, 18.8% of physician reference facts have identified support in the prior evidence, compared with 65.4% and 63.5% of facts generated by a general-purpose and a medically specialized model. Overlap is substantially higher for supported content (0.255 and 0.236) than for content without identified support (0.030 and 0.026). The two scores are weakly correlated across admissions (rho = 0.22 and 0.17), and conventional metrics do not consistently capture both dimensions. FairSumEval distinguishes evidence-grounded summarization from agreement on content without identified support, revealing what models omit and add in each category.
articles.summary: FairSumEval은 퇴원 요약문의 사실을 모델 입력에서 근거가 확인되는 내용과 그렇지 않은 내용으로 나눠 평가하는 프레임워크다. MIMIC-III 입원 사례 200건에서 의사 작성 참조문의 사실 중 선행 기록에서 근거가 확인된 비율은 18.8%였고, 두 모델 생성문의 해당 비율은 각각 65.4%와 63.5%였다. 이는 의사 요약이 부정확하다는 뜻이 아니라 퇴원 시점의 판단이나 인계 정보처럼 모델 입력에 없는 내용이 참조문에 포함될 수 있음을 보여준다. 의료 요약 시스템을 평가할 때 근거 있는 정보의 누락과 입력에 없는 내용의 재현 실패를 구분해야 한다는 실무적 함의가 있다.

articles.title: 이모션웨이브, AI 기반 공간 미디어 플랫폼 공개…日, XR·로보틱스 시장 진출 추진
articles.content:
AI 인프라 전문기업 이모션웨이브(대표 장순철)가 일본에서 확장현실(XR) 기반 공간 미디어 플랫폼을 선보이고, 자체 인공지능(AI) 인프라 기술을 활용한 해외 사업 확대에 나섰다. 콘텐츠 제작과 처리, 서비스 운영을 연결하는 인공지능 인프라를 XR과 로보틱스 분야에 적용하는 것이 핵심이다.

이모션웨이브는 지난 11일부터 13일까지 일본 마쿠하리 멧세(Makuhari Messe)에서 열린 '2026 도쿄 XR 페어(XR Fair Tokyo 2026 Autumn)'에 참가해 리마엔터테인먼트와 공동으로 공간 미디어 플랫폼 '나루(NARU)'를 소개했다.

나루는 애플 비전 프로(Apple Vision Pro)를 기반으로 가상 공간에서 영상과 디지털 콘텐츠를 몰입감 있게 경험할 수 있도록 설계된 플랫폼이다. 생성형 AI와 XR 기술을 결합해 기존 영상 콘텐츠를 공간형 미디어 서비스로 확장하는 데 초점을 맞췄다.

전시 현장에서는 야마하(Yamaha), 캐논(Canon), 도요타(Toyota) 등 일본 주요 기업 관계자들이 시연에 참여해 공간 미디어 기술의 활용 가능성을 살펴봤다. 이모션웨이브는 나루 프로젝트의 공식 홈페이지도 공개했으며, 향후 다양한 증강현실(AR)·XR 기기와 AI 글래스로 서비스 적용 범위를 넓힐 계획이다.

나루의 기반 기술은 이모션웨이브가 자체 개발한 AI 인프라 솔루션 '에임플(AIMPLE)'이다. 이 솔루션은 AI 콘텐츠 생성과 처리, 미디어 서비스 운영을 연결하는 통합 인프라로, 기업이 AI 기반 미디어 서비스를 구축하고 운영할 수 있도록 지원하는 것을 목표로 한다.

이모션웨이브는 일본 방문 기간에 야마하 주식회사(Yamaha Corporation), 니혼 XR 센터(NIHON XR CENTER INC.), 알파시스템즈(Alpha Systems), 키카가쿠(KIKAGAKU Inc.) 등 현지 기업 관계자들과도 비즈니스 미팅을 진행했다.

협의에서는 에임플을 활용한 AI 모델 학습·추론 환경 구축과 산업별 AI 서비스 적용 방안을 논의했다. 특히 로보틱스와 XR 분야에서 인프라 기술을 적용하고, 향후 기술 실증과 공동 사업화로 연결할 수 있는 가능성을 검토했다.

이모션웨이브는 이번 전시와 현지 기업 교류를 계기로 일본을 비롯한 해외 시장에서 AI 인프라와 공간 미디어 기술의 적용 분야를 확대할 방침이다. 다만 현재까지 공개된 협력 내용은 기술 적용 및 사업화 가능성에 관한 논의 단계로, 구체적인 공동 개발 계약이나 상용화 성과는 발표되지 않았다.

이모션웨이브 관계자는 "AI 인프라의 경쟁력은 연산 자원 확보를 넘어 실제 산업과 서비스에 적용할 수 있는 기술 역량에 있다"며 "일본 전시에서 확인한 나루의 활용 가능성과 현지 기업들과의 협력을 바탕으로 에임플의 글로벌 사업 영역을 확대하겠다"고 밝혔다.
